analysis.one_liner: Limits company stock in 401(k) plans, bans trading blackouts on employee savings, and requires three-year vesting of employee contributions.
analysis.headline: Introduced after the Enron collapse exposed workers' 401(k) losses, the bill never got a hearing or a vote and died when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have restricted 401(k) plans from holding too much of a worker's own savings in their employer's company stock, required plans to let workers move their own contributions into diversified investments at least quarterly, banned the temporary 'blackout' freezes that block workers from selling, and made employee contributions fully vested after three years of service. It also created criminal and civil penalties for plan officials who violate those rules. It was written after the Enron bankruptcy, where employees locked out of selling during a plan freeze watched their retirement savings evaporate with company stock.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers in 401(k) plans, especially at companies that match contributions in company stock or encourage employees to hold it. They would gain the right to diversify their own contributions at least quarterly, protection from account freezes, guaranteed ownership of their own contributions after three years, and new penalties against plan officials who violate these rules.
analysis.who_benefits_short: 401(k) savers, especially employees holding company stock

how_it_helps.text: Caps the amount of a participant's employee contributions that a 401(k) plan may invest in employer securities at 20 percent, unless the worker affirmatively elected the investment.
Requires plans to give participants a reasonable opportunity, at least quarterly, to move accrued employee contributions out of employer stock into diversified investments.

Prohibits plan sponsors, administrators, and fiduciaries from imposing any lockdown, blackout, or freeze on a participant's ability to transfer nonforfeitable accrued benefits out of employer securities.
Makes 100 percent of employee elective deferrals nonforfeitable (vested) after three years of plan participation, amending both ERISA and the Internal Revenue Code.

Adds criminal penalties of up to $5,000 and one year in prison for individuals (fines up to $100,000 for entities) who willfully violate the new rules, and lets the Labor Secretary assess civil penalties of up to $1,000 per day per affected participant until a violation is corrected.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that sponsor 401(k) plans and pay part of compensation in company stock would bear compliance costs and lose the ability to steer employee savings into company shares. Plan administrators and fiduciaries would face new compliance duties and penalty exposure. Companies would also lose the capital-raising and loyalty benefits of workers holding company stock in their retirement accounts.

drawbacks.text: Compliance burden: employers and plan administrators would have to restructure plan investment menus, monitor the 20 percent cap per participant, and process quarterly diversification elections, with penalty exposure of up to $1,000 per day per affected participant for violations.

Companies that match 401(k) contributions with employer stock, or use broad employee stock ownership as part of their pay structure, would have to redesign their compensation approach, and some argue employees benefit from ownership of the company they build.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections directly targeted a demonstrated harm: workers whose retirement savings were concentrated in employer stock and frozen during a trading blackout while the company collapsed. The compliance costs on employers are real but conventional — the same kind of duties ERISA already imposes. The bill's cap applied to employee contributions (with an opt-out), not employer matches, which limits how disruptive it would be. A fair reading is that the worker benefits outweighed the compliance burden, though the penalty regime was strict.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on February 5, 2002, referred to two House committees, sent to a subcommittee in May, and never moved again before the Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Rep. Phil English introduced the bill on February 5, 2002, and it was referred to both the Education and the Workforce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee.
On May 9, 2002, the portion in the Education and the Workforce Committee was referred to its Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations, a step short of a full-committee markup or floor vote.
No further action was recorded; the bill received no hearing-driven markup, no floor vote, and no Senate counterpart action before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that sponsor 401(k) plans — particularly companies that match in company stock or encourage employee ownership — were better off because the bill died: they avoided the 20 percent cap on employee contributions in company stock, the ban on lockdowns, mandatory quarterly diversification rights, three-year vesting of deferrals, and the new criminal and civil penalties. Plan administrators avoided the compliance and penalty regime as well.

against.name: John Boehner
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup after its referral and subcommittee referral; the House instead took up a competing, narrower pension-security bill that he backed.

against.name: Bill Thomas
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Ways and Means
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill referred to his committee; no markup or vote was ever scheduled there.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Republican with one Democratic and one Republican cosponsor, so the two-person sponsorship was bipartisan but tiny; no vote was ever recorded, so partisan positions cannot be measured from the record.

industries.industry: Employers sponsoring 401(k) plans (especially those matching in company stock)
industries.note: The bill would have capped employee savings held in company stock, banned lockdowns that trap workers during a freeze, and imposed penalties. Companies lose flexibility to steer employee savings into their own shares — a flexibility that cost Enron workers their retirement savings when a blackout froze selling while the stock collapsed.
They would face new compliance duties and penalty exposure of up to $1,000 per day per affected participant, but they are also the parties whose fiduciary failures the penalties exist to deter.

industries.industry: Diversified investment vehicles (mutual funds and similar)
industries.note: Quarterly diversification rights would have moved employee money out of single-stock concentration into diversified funds, increasing assets under their management.
